entry: Highly contagious bacterial respiratory disease caused by *Bordetella pertussis*, also called pertussis or the 100-day cough. It begins with symptoms like a [[Common cold|common cold]], followed after one or two weeks by violent coughing fits that often end in a high-pitched whoop as the person inhales. The cough usually lasts 1–6 weeks but can last 10 or more. Infants may have little or no cough and instead pause in breathing. Among infected children under one year old, about 50% need hospitalization and nearly 0.5% (1 in 200) die. Prevention is mainly by [[Vaccination|vaccination]] with the pertussis vaccine, given as four doses in the first two years of life, with additional doses for older children and adults. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] are useful if started within three weeks of symptoms but otherwise have little effect. In 2015 an estimated 16.3 million people were infected and 58,700 died, down from 138,000 deaths in 1990.

Family of wireless network protocols based on the IEEE 802.11 standards. Wi-Fi lets nearby digital devices exchange data by [[Radio wave|radio waves]] and provides Internet access through [[Router (computing)|wireless routers]] and access points in homes, offices and public places. The name is a trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance, which certifies products that pass interoperability testing. Over 3.05 billion Wi-Fi-enabled devices were shipped globally each year as of 2019. Wi-Fi is designed to work with its wired counterpart, [[Ethernet]]. It usually operates in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, with 6 GHz used in newer generations, and an access point's indoor range is about 20 m (66 ft). As of 2025, some versions reach 23 Gbit/s at close range.

Modern pagan, syncretic, Earth-focused religion. It developed in England during the first half of the 20th century from [[Western esotericism|Western esoteric]] traditions, and Gerald Gardner, a retired British civil servant, introduced it to the public in 1954. Doreen Valiente joined him in the 1950s and helped build its liturgical tradition. Scholars of religion classify Wicca as a [[New religious movement|new religious movement]] and a form of modern paganism. It is typically duotheistic, venerating a goddess and a god, traditionally the Triple Goddess and the Horned God. Celebrations follow the cycles of the Moon, called Esbats, and seasonal festivals of the Sun, called Sabbats. The Wiccan Rede is a popular expression of Wiccan morality, often linked to the ritual practice of [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]]. Some Wiccans prefer the word spirituality to religion.

City (pop., 2020: 397,532), county seat of Sedgwick County in south-central Kansas, on the Arkansas River. Wichita began as a trading post on the Chisholm Trail in the 1860s and was incorporated in 1870. As a stop for cattle drives from Texas, it earned the nickname Cowtown. In 1875 [[Wyatt Earp]] served as a police officer there. In the 1920s and 1930s aircraft makers were established in the city, which became known as The Air Capital of the World. [[Airbus]] and [[Boeing]] still operate facilities there. Its airport, Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, is the largest in Kansas.

Musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Schwartz and a book by Winnie Holzman. Loosely based on Gregory Maguire's 1995 novel, it reimagines *The Wonderful Wizard of Oz* through the relationship of Elphaba and Glinda, the future Wicked Witch of the West and Glinda the Good. It premiered on Broadway in October 2003 after tryouts in San Francisco. The original cast included [[Idina Menzel]] as Elphaba and Kristin Chenoweth as Glinda. The show won three Tony Awards, and in 2017 it surpassed *The Phantom of the Opera* to become Broadway's second-highest-grossing musical, as of 2026. A two-part film adaptation was released in 2024 and 2025.

Female spouse; a woman in a marital relationship. She remains a wife until her marriage is legally dissolved by divorce or until her partner dies, when she becomes a widow. Her rights, obligations and status vary between cultures and have changed over time. The word derives from Proto-Germanic *wībam*, meaning woman, and the older sense survives in *midwife*. Many cultures expect a married woman to take her husband's surname. The term applies to a woman in a union sanctioned by law, including religious law, but usually not to an informal [[Cohabitation|cohabiting]] partner, though a woman in a [[Common law|common-law]] marriage may use it. An annulment, unlike a [[Divorce|divorce]], is usually retroactive, so the marriage is treated as never having existed. Many countries are replacing wife and husband with spouse in their statute law.

Head covering made from human or animal hair, or a synthetic imitation. Wigs may be worn to disguise baldness, alter appearance, or as part of certain professional uniforms. Ancient Egyptians wore wigs to shield shaved heads from the sun, fixing them with beeswax and resin. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, wigs fell out of use in the West for about a thousand years. Their revival in the 16th century helped with hair loss and reduced head lice. [[Louis XIII]] began wearing one in 1624 after premature balding, and his successor [[Louis XIV]] promoted the fashion across Europe. Men's wig-wearing dominated for about 140 years, until dress changed in the 1790s under the influence of the [[French Revolution]].

Home video game console by [[Nintendo]]. Released on November 19, 2006, in North America, it was Nintendo's fifth major home console and a seventh-generation console alongside the [[Xbox 360]] and [[PlayStation 3]]. Its wireless Wii Remote detects motion and gestures. Nintendo's focus on play rather than raw computing power kept production costs low. The bundled game Wii Sports became its killer app. Lifetime sales exceed 101 million units, making it the seventh-best-selling console of all time as of April 2026. Production ended in October 2013. Its successor, the Wii U, became Nintendo's worst-selling home console.

Non-profit media organization that publishes leaked documents from whistleblowers. Founded in 2006 by [[Julian Assange]], it says its website has released more than ten million documents. Its releases include a video of a 2007 US helicopter strike in Baghdad, titled Collateral Murder, which killed Reuters journalists; thousands of US military logs from Afghanistan and Iraq; and CIA hacking tools. During the 2016 US presidential campaign it released emails from the Democratic National Committee and from [[Hillary Clinton]]'s campaign manager, which contributed to the chairwoman's resignation. Critics cite inadequate curation, privacy violations and bias. In 2023 Assange said WikiLeaks could no longer publish because of his imprisonment and surveillance pressures.

Type of website whose pages its audience can edit directly through a web browser, with little structure imposed by a defined owner or leader. The name derives from the Hawaiian word meaning quick, and from WikiWikiWeb, the first user-editable website. Ward Cunningham, developer of the first wiki software, described a wiki as the simplest online database that could possibly work. Wikis are used for knowledge management, note-taking and community sites. The most popular is [[Wikipedia]], which is a collection of hundreds of wikis in different languages. Wiki engines range from free and open-source software to proprietary products.

Free online encyclopedia written and maintained by volunteer editors. It was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001 as a [[Wiki|wiki]] complement to Nupedia, an expert-written encyclopedia project. It has been hosted since 2003 by the Wikimedia Foundation, an American nonprofit funded mainly by reader donations. It is the largest and most read reference work in history. As of November 2026 the English edition has more than seven million articles, and all editions together exceed 68 million. Its reliability was often criticized in the 2000s but has earned more praise since the late 2010s. Critics point to systemic [[Bias|bias]], including gender bias against women and geographic bias against the Global South. Some national governments have censored it, from specific pages to the entire site.

American frontier scout, lawman and gambler, also a showman and actor. Raised on an [[Illinois|Illinois]] farm, he headed west as a young man and worked as a stagecoach driver and lawman in Kansas and Nebraska. He served as a scout and spy for the Union army in the [[American Civil War]]. Many tales of his exploits were exaggerated or fabricated, some by himself. His biographer Joseph G. Rosa credits him with killing six or seven men between 1861 and 1871. In Deadwood, Dakota Territory (now [[South Dakota]]), he was shot and killed by Jack McCall while playing [[Poker|poker]]. The hand he supposedly held, black aces and eights, became known as the dead man's hand.

Species of suid (*Sus scrofa*), also known as the wild swine. It is native to much of Eurasia and North Africa, has been introduced to the Americas and Oceania, and is one of the widest-ranging mammals. It is listed as least concern by the IUCN but has become [[Invasive species|invasive]] in part of its introduced range. As of 2005, up to 16 subspecies are recognized. Wild boars live in matriarchal groups of related females and their young, while adult males are usually solitary outside the breeding season. The [[Wolf|wolf]] is its main predator across most of its range. The species is the ancestor of most domestic [[Pig|pig]] breeds. Boar–pig [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] have become serious pests in the Americas and Australia.

Upland game bird native to North America, one of two extant turkey species and the heaviest member of the order [[Galliformes]]. It is the ancestor of the [[Domestic turkey|domestic turkey]], which derives from a southern Mexican subspecies. Adult males, called toms, normally weigh 5 to 11 kg (11 to 24 lb), and the record male weighed 17.06 kg (37.6 lb). Mature males have a reddish, featherless head and a fleshy snood on the bill. In late winter males display and gobble to attract mates. Overhunting brought the bird near extinction by the early 20th century. Reintroductions from the 1940s restored it to all U.S. states except Alaska.

[[Antelope|Antelope]] of the genus *Connochaetes*, native to eastern and southern Africa. There are two species: the blue wildebeest, also called the brindled gnu, and the black wildebeest or white-tailed gnu. The two diverged about one million years ago. In East Africa the blue wildebeest is the most abundant big-game species, and some populations make an annual migration to new grazing grounds. Calves are born at the end of the rainy season and must move with the herd soon after birth, and some fall prey to spotted hyenas. Wildebeest often graze with [[Zebra|zebras]], which heightens awareness of predators. They compete with livestock for pasture, and farmers sometimes blame them for spreading disease to [[Cattle|cattle]]. Both species are listed as least concern by the IUCN. The name is Afrikaans for wild beast, wild ox or wild cattle.

Unplanned, uncontrolled fire in an area of combustible vegetation. Some natural forest ecosystems depend on wildfire, and many plant species rely on fire for growth and reproduction. Forest managers use prescribed burns to reduce fire risk, although controlled burns can escape containment. Ignition comes from natural causes such as [[Lightning|lightning]], volcanic eruptions and spontaneous combustion, or from human activity, which is responsible for over 85% of wildfires in the United States. Severe fires often follow wet periods that build fuel and then [[Drought|drought]] and heat, and [[Climate change|climate change]] has intensified these cycles. Human practices have caused a doubling in land area burned compared with natural levels. Wildfire releases [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], which adds to the greenhouse effect and creates a climate feedback.

Protection of wild species and their [[Habitat|habitats]] to maintain healthy populations and to restore or enhance natural ecosystems. Major threats include habitat destruction, overexploitation, poaching, pollution, climate change and the illegal wildlife trade. The IUCN estimates that 42,100 of the species it has assessed are at risk of extinction, and a 2019 UN report on biodiversity put the figure at a million species. Deforestation for agriculture or logging removes habitat for more than 80% of the world's species, which live in forests. Key agreements include the 1973 Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and the 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity. Nongovernmental groups include the Nature Conservancy, World Wildlife Fund and Conservation International.

Last German emperor and king of Prussia (r. 1888–1918). He was the eldest of the 42 grandchildren of [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]]. In 1890 he dismissed Chancellor [[Otto von Bismarck|Otto von Bismarck]] and assumed direct control of policy. His reign saw Germany acquire territory in China and the Pacific and become Europe's largest manufacturer. His tactless foreign policy, including a massive naval buildup, alienated most of Europe, and many consider it a cause of the empire's fall. In 1914 he guaranteed military support to Austria-Hungary during the July Crisis, which helped plunge Europe into [[World War I|World War I]]. He left most war decisions to the German Supreme Army Command, which dominated policy from 1916. Forced to abdicate during the German Revolution, he went into exile in the Netherlands, where he died.

King of Prussia (r. 1861–88) and first German emperor (r. 1871–88). He was not expected to inherit the throne, but became heir presumptive in 1840. He played a major role in crushing the Revolutions of 1848 in Germany and was briefly exiled in England. After coming into conflict with the Landtag over military budgets, he appointed [[Otto von Bismarck|Otto von Bismarck]] minister president, beginning a partnership that lasted his life. Prussia won the [[Austro-Prussian War|Austro-Prussian War]] and, after the [[Franco-Prussian War|Franco-Prussian War]], German unification was achieved in 1871. Wilhelm largely left governance to Bismarck. He was succeeded by his son Frederick, who died after 99 days, and the throne passed to [[Wilhelm II|Wilhelm II]].

German experimental physicist. In 1895, while working at the University of Würzburg, he investigated electromagnetic radiation and found a wavelength range now called [[X-ray|X-rays]] (Röntgen rays in many languages). He noticed that the rays passed through objects and made images on photographic plates. In 1901 he became the first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics. He refused to patent the technology, and he held professorships at several German universities, ending at [[Munich|Munich]]. The element roentgenium is named in his honor.

German physiologist and philosopher, widely regarded as the father of experimental psychology. He was the first person to call himself a psychologist, and he distinguished psychology as a science from philosophy and biology. In 1879, at the University of [[Leipzig|Leipzig]], he founded the first formal laboratory for psychological research. He also established the first academic journal for psychological research and wrote the 1874 textbook *Principles of Physiological Psychology*. He studied the elements of [[Consciousness|consciousness]] such as sensation and feeling using introspection. A 1991 survey of American historians ranked him first for all-time eminence, ahead of [[William James|William James]] and [[Sigmund Freud|Sigmund Freud]].

American cartoonist, writer and entrepreneur. Born in [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn]] to Jewish immigrant parents, he grew up poor and was one of the earliest cartoonists in the American comic book industry. His series *The Spirit* (1940–1952) was noted for its experiments in content and form. In 1978 he popularized the term graphic novel with *A Contract with God*. He later wrote *Comics and Sequential Art* (1985), an early contribution to formal comics studies. He co-founded the Eisner-Iger Studio, which packaged content for early comic books. The Eisner Award is named in his honor.

American actor, comedian, writer and producer. He first gained prominence on [[Saturday Night Live|Saturday Night Live]] from 1995 to 2002 and then starred in comedy films such as *Elf* (2003), *Anchorman* (2004), *Talladega Nights* (2006) and *Step Brothers* (2008). He co-founded the comedy website Funny or Die in 2007 with Adam McKay. He has also taken dramatic roles, including in *Stranger than Fiction* (2006). He has won several Primetime Emmy Awards as a producer, including for the drama series *Succession*. In 2015 he received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame|Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American actor, rapper and film producer. He first gained recognition in the hip-hop duo DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince and starred as a fictionalized version of himself in *The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air* (1990–1996). His film franchises include *Bad Boys* and *Men in Black*, and his films as a leading man have grossed over $10 billion. He was nominated for an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for *Ali* (2001) and *The Pursuit of Happyness* (2006), and won the award for *King Richard* (2021). At the 94th Academy Awards he slapped presenter [[Chris Rock|Chris Rock]], then resigned from the Academy and was banned from its events for ten years.

Legal document expressing a person's wishes for the distribution of property after death. It also names an executor to manage the estate until final distribution, and it may create a testamentary [[Trust (law)|trust]] that takes effect only after death. The phrase comes from English law, when Old English and Law French were used side by side, and records show the terms were used interchangeably for personal and real property. Plutarch credited [[Solon|Solon]] with inventing the written will. [[Civil law (legal system)|Civil law]] systems often restrict freedom of disposition, for example through forced heirship. Holographic wills, handwritten by the testator, need not be witnessed, while nuncupative wills, which are oral, were often limited to sailors or military personnel.
